central_question: Would one officer trust the machine, or the evidence that the machine was wrong?
audience_promise: A real nuclear false alarm, one human judgment under impossible pressure, and the quiet consequence of refusing to escalate uncertainty.
impossible_event: A Soviet early-warning system reported five American missiles even though no missiles were launched.
human_anchor: Lieutenant Colonel Stanislav Petrov had minutes to decide whether to trust the warning or the evidence that contradicted it.
causal_hinge: Petrov reported the alert as false instead of passing it forward as a confirmed attack.
causal_chain: The Soviet early-warning system reports an American missile launch.
The system escalates the report from one missile to five.
Ground radar does not confirm the satellite warning.
Petrov reports the alarm as false.
The signal is traced to sunlight reflected from high clouds.
The system failure is exposed and Petrov's career suffers.
visual_representation_by_stage: Dark bunker panel; red warning indicator comes alive.
Representational command-bunker portrait/composition of Petrov; no false archival claim.
Alert moves through a command-chain diagram.
One launch indicator becomes two, then three.
Counter reaches five; alarm intensity rises.
Petrov studies the panel, telephone and clock.
Ground radar remains empty while satellite alert flashes.
False-alarm classification is entered; no celebratory interface.
Bunker waits; clock advances through silence.
Empty night sky; expected impact never occurs.
Sunlight geometry over high clouds and satellite sensor.
Declassified report/logbook treatment with readable evidence cues.
Petrov's later obscurity represented through empty military corridor.
Red warning fades into neutral black; no victory imagery.
Final branded logo lockup with restrained red pulse.
irreversible_choice: Report the alert as false instead of passing it forward as a confirmed attack.
payoff: He refused to turn uncertainty into a catastrophe; the historically accurate payoff is quieter than the later mythology.

opening_sentence: Just after midnight on September 26, 1983, a Soviet early-warning system reported five American nuclear missiles in the air.

question_answers.what_happened: The Soviet early-warning system reported five missiles that were not actually launched.
question_answers.why_it_happened: Sunlight reflecting from high clouds was misread by the satellite warning system.
question_answers.who_was_affected: Petrov, the Soviet command chain and the wider world exposed to the danger of escalation.
question_answers.what_changed_everything: Petrov classified the alert as false instead of escalating it as a confirmed attack.
question_answers.why_it_seems_impossible: A machine reported a nuclear attack while the physical evidence did not support one.
question_answers.proof_or_source_note: The account is anchored in institutional history, an archival document record and technical false-alarm analysis.
question_answers.how_danger_grows: The system escalates from one reported launch to five, while the decision window narrows.
question_answers.irreversible_consequence: Passing the alert forward as real could have moved the command toward retaliation; the exact counterfactual is not claimed as certain.
question_answers.visual_representation_by_stage: Each narrative stage has a distinct representational, diagrammatic or documentary-treatment shot assignment.
question_answers.first_frame_promise: The viewer immediately sees a warning system report five missiles before learning why the report was wrong.
